name: Action without attachment to results
summary: Krishna's counsel that one's responsibility lies in the action itself — done well and for the right reasons — rather than in controlling its outcome. It is not indifference to results or a licence for careless work: the same passages ask for steady, skilful effort (2.48, 2.50). The Isha Upanishad likewise speaks of a full life lived "performing Karma (righteous deeds)" without being defiled by it (Isha 2).
caveats: Spoken to Arjuna about his duty in a specific war; applying it to modern work and study is an interpretation.
life_situations: anxiety about exam or interview results
obsessing over outcomes you cannot control

name: Steadiness in success and failure
summary: Evenness of mind toward pleasure and pain, gain and loss, honour and dishonour. The Gita presents it as a discipline cultivated while acting ("equilibrium is called yoga", 2.48), not as emotional numbness.
life_situations: being thrown off balance by praise and blame

name: One's own path (svadharma)
summary: "Better one's own duty, though destitute of merit, than the duty of another, well discharged" (3.35, repeated in 18.47). It discourages taking up another's path because it looks more successful.
caveats: In the text, svadharma refers to duties tied to one's social station and nature (Arjuna's is the warrior's). Reading it as following one's individual calling is a modern interpretation.
It must never be used to justify caste discrimination or to keep anyone in a role they did not choose.
life_situations: comparing your career path with friends
pressure to follow someone else's choices
choosing a field that fits who you are

name: Paralysis before a hard choice
summary: The Gita opens with Arjuna overwhelmed: he sees kinsmen on both sides, his body fails him, and he cannot tell what is right. His despair is taken seriously — the whole teaching answers it — and his turning point is to admit his confusion and ask for guidance (2.7).
caveats: Arjuna's words in chapter 1 and early chapter 2 describe his despair; they are not teachings to follow.
life_situations: a decision where every option hurts someone

name: Training the restless mind
summary: Arjuna objects that the mind is as hard to curb as the wind; Krishna agrees, and answers that it can be trained "by constant practice and by dispassion" (6.35). Whenever the mind wanders, bring it back (6.26). The Katha Upanishad pictures the body as a chariot, the intellect as its driver, "mind the reins" and the senses as horses (Katha 1.3.3-1.3.6).

name: How desire turns into anger
summary: A chain of causes: dwelling on objects breeds attachment, attachment desire, desire anger; anger brings delusion, confused memory and the loss of reason (2.62–2.63). Desire and wrath are named as "our foe here on earth" (3.37).

name: The person of steady wisdom
summary: Arjuna asks how a person of stable mind speaks, sits and walks (2.54). Krishna's answer describes someone untroubled in sorrow, without craving in pleasure, free of fear and anger, content in the Self, and at peace (2.55–2.72).

name: Grief and what does not perish
summary: Krishna answers Arjuna's grief by teaching that the dweller in the body is not born and does not die (2.20); bodies are cast off like worn-out garments (2.22); death is certain for the born (2.27). Death teaches Nachiketas the same in the Katha Upanishad: "This Self is never born, nor does It die" (Katha 1.2.18).
caveats: In context, this is said to a warrior grieving in advance of a battle.
These verses concern the nature of the self. They should never be used to dismiss someone's grief; the Gita itself begins with grief taken seriously.

name: Enduring what comes and goes
summary: Contacts that give cold and heat, pleasure and pain "come and go, impermanent; endure them bravely" (2.14). Pleasures born of contact have a beginning and an end (5.22).

name: Courage and fearlessness
summary: Krishna rouses Arjuna from faint-heartedness — "Shake off this paltry faint-heartedness! Stand up" (2.3) — and lists fearlessness first among the divine qualities (16.1). Even a little of this knowledge "protects from great fear" (2.40). The Katha Upanishad calls out in the same spirit: "Arise! Awake!" (Katha 1.3.14).
caveats: Many of Krishna's exhortations urge Arjuna to fight a specific war; they are not an endorsement of violence or of ignoring real danger.

name: No sincere effort is wasted
summary: "In this there is no loss of effort" (2.40). Arjuna asks what becomes of one who strives but falls short; Krishna answers that "never doth any who worketh righteousness … tread the path of woe" (6.40), and that such a person recovers their former progress and labours on (6.43–6.44).
caveats: In 6.40–6.45 the carrying-forward of effort is described across lifetimes; applying it within a single career or exam season is an interpretation.
life_situations: feeling that your effort was wasted

name: Be a friend to yourself
summary: "Let him raise the self by the Self and not let the self become depressed; for verily is the Self the friend of the self, and also the Self the self's enemy" (6.5). Self-mastery is what makes the self a friend (6.6).

name: Envy, comparison and goodwill
summary: The wise are described as free from envy (4.22), bearing no ill-will to any being (12.13), and content (12.14); "absence of envy and pride" is among the divine qualities (16.3). Together with 3.35 this points toward measuring yourself by your own duty rather than by others' gains.

name: Contentment
summary: "Ever content" and "wholly content with what cometh" recur in the portraits of the wise and the devoted (12.14, 12.19). In 12.14 contentment sits beside being "resolute": it is not the absence of effort. The Isha Upanishad opens with the same counsel: "Do not covet the wealth of any man" (Isha 1).

name: Moderation in daily life
summary: Yoga is not for one who eats or sleeps too much or too little (6.16); it "killeth out all pain for him who is regulated in eating and amusement, regulated in performing actions, regulated in sleeping and waking" (6.17).

name: Leading by example
summary: "Whatsoever a great man doeth, that other men also do" (3.21). The wise act with "an eye to the welfare of the world" (3.20, 3.25) and do not unsettle the minds of others, but show the way by their own conduct (3.26).
life_situations: being a role model for younger people

name: Truthful and kind speech
summary: The "austerity of speech" is speech "causing no annoyance, truthful, pleasant and beneficial" (17.15); the austerity of the mind includes serenity and self-control (17.16).
life_situations: conflict with a partner, parent or friend

name: Friendliness and compassion
summary: The devotee dear to Krishna "beareth no ill-will to any being, friendly and compassionate … and forgiving" (12.13), "alike to foe and friend" (12.18). 6.9 praises one who regards friends, foes and strangers impartially.
caveats: Being "alike to foe and friend" describes inner steadiness and goodwill. It does not require trusting someone who has harmed you or staying in an unsafe situation.
life_situations: dealing with someone who hurt you

name: Forgiveness and forbearance
summary: Forgiveness (kṣamā) is among the divine qualities (16.3) and among the states of beings that arise from Krishna (10.4); forgiveness (kṣānti) is also listed among the marks of wisdom (13.8).
caveats: Forgiveness does not mean excusing abuse, staying in harm's way, or giving up appropriate boundaries.
life_situations: being unable to let go of a wrong

name: Lust, anger and greed
summary: "Triple is the gate of this hell, destructive of the self—lust, wrath, and greed" (16.21); one freed from them "accomplisheth his own welfare" (16.22).

name: Faith (śraddhā)
summary: "The man consists of his faith; that which his faith is, he is even that" (17.3). Faith with mastery of the senses leads to wisdom (4.39); for "the doubting self" there is no happiness (4.40).

name: Cutting through doubt
summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to cleave "ignorance-born doubt" with "the sword of the wisdom of the Self" and stand up (4.42). Arjuna ends the dialogue: "Destroyed is my delusion … my doubts have fled away" (18.73).

name: Taking refuge, letting go
summary: Krishna's closing teaching invites Arjuna to come to him "for shelter" and "sorrow not" (18.66), and promises security to those devoted to him (9.22).
caveats: These are devotional teachings within a theistic framework; readers relate to them in different ways.
How "abandoning all duties" in 18.66 should be understood is debated among commentators. It is not a call to passivity — the dialogue ends with Arjuna acting.
life_situations: needing to let go of control

name: Devotion (bhakti)
summary: Devotion is presented as open to anyone: "a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water" offered with devotion is accepted (9.26), and whatever one does can be an offering (9.27).
life_situations: finding the sacred in daily work

name: Not running away from responsibility
summary: Freedom does not come from abstaining from action (3.4); no one can remain actionless (3.5), and action is better than inaction (3.8). Giving up a duty merely because it is painful is not true relinquishment (18.8); true relinquishment is giving up attachment to the fruit (18.2).
caveats: Not every decision to leave is escapism. Leaving a harmful job, relationship or course of study can be the responsible choice.
life_situations: wanting to quit when things get hard

name: The three qualities (guṇas)
summary: Nature acts through three qualities — Harmony (sattva), Motion (rajas) and Inertia (tamas) — which bind in different ways (14.5–14.8); wisdom arises from the first, greed from the second, heedlessness from the third (14.17).

name: Short-term pleasure and lasting good
summary: Three kinds of pleasure: one which "at first is as venom but in the end is as nectar" (18.37), one at first as nectar but in the end like venom (18.38), and one deluding from start to finish (18.39). Contact-born delights are "wombs of pain" (5.22). The Katha Upanishad draws the same line: "The good is one thing and the pleasant another" (Katha 1.2.1).
life_situations: choosing between fun now and goals later

name: Learning with humility
summary: "Learn thou this by discipleship, by investigation, and by service" (4.34). Humility and unpretentiousness head the list of what counts as wisdom (13.8). "Arise! Awake! Having reached the Great Ones (illumined Teachers), gain understanding" (Katha 1.3.14).

name: Ego and humility
summary: "The self, deluded by egoism" takes itself to be the doer (3.27). Hypocrisy, arrogance and conceit are named among the demoniacal properties (16.4), and Arjuna's "I will not fight" is called a resolve "entrenched in egoism" (18.59).
life_situations: taking all the credit or all the blame

name: Reflect fully, then choose
summary: After the whole teaching Krishna tells Arjuna: "having reflected on it fully, then act thou as thou listest" (18.63). The guidance is offered for reflection, and the decision remains Arjuna's own.
life_situations: wanting someone else to decide for you

name: Qualities worth cultivating
summary: Chapter 16 lists the qualities of one "born with the divine properties" — fearlessness, purity, almsgiving, self-restraint, harmlessness, truth, absence of wrath, compassion, mildness, modesty, forgiveness, fortitude — and contrasts them with hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, wrath and harshness.
life_situations: deciding what kind of person to be

name: Skill and meaning in work
summary: "Yoga is skill in action" (2.50). A person reaches perfection by being intent on their own work (18.45) and by worshipping through it (18.46); whatever one does can be offered (9.27).

name: Meditation practice
summary: Chapter 6 describes meditation: a secluded place, a steady seat, the mind made one-pointed (6.10–6.12), "as a lamp in a windless place" that does not flicker (6.19).

name: The senses and their pull
summary: The roving senses can hurry the understanding away "as the gale hurries away a ship upon the waters" (2.67); the wise withdraw them as a tortoise draws in its limbs (2.58). Attraction and aversion lie in wait in the senses (3.34).

name: Seeing all beings equally
summary: Sages "look equally" on a learned Brahmana, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste (5.18); the harmonised self sees the Self in all beings (6.29) and "seeth equality in everything" through the likeness of the Self (6.32). The Isha Upanishad describes one who "sees all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings" (Isha 6).
caveats: Besant's 1922 wording reflects the social vocabulary of its time.

name: Many factors shape an outcome
summary: Krishna names five causes of every action — "the body, the actor, the various organs, the diverse kinds of energies, and the presiding deities also, the fifth" (18.14, Besant). Regarding oneself as the sole actor is called a failure of understanding (18.16).
caveats: Translations differ on the fifth factor (daiva). Besant renders it "the presiding deities"; others understand it as providence or fate.
life_situations: blaming yourself entirely for a failure
